title: The Nobel poet
hookLine: Rabindranath Tagore won the Nobel Prize in 1913 for Gitanjali, "song offerings"
tomorrow: what did Tagore see one morning, standing on a Calcutta street?

lines: A BRIEFCASE LEFT ON THE UNDERGROUND.
cards: Left something on a train once? Rabindranath Tagore's son told this story on himself.
In London, the son left a briefcase on the Underground, and in it was a notebook of his father's poems, put into English by the poet himself. The next day, lost property had it.
Inside were the songs the world would come to know as Gitanjali. A lost notebook, and very nearly a lost book.

teach.b: Tagore wrote in Bengali, and these were his own English prose versions of his devotional songs. The Irish poet Yeats wrote the introduction to the English book, whose title page calls it Song Offerings.
In 1913, the Nobel Prize in Literature went to Tagore. Here's how the second song opens: "When thou commandest me to sing it seems that my heart would break with pride." Notice who he sings to.

teach.h: SUNG TO THOU, NEVER A STATUE.
teach.b: Thou: a friend, a master, a lover, never given a statue. That walks right into an old debate in Indian devotion.
Tagore grew up in the Brahmo Samaj, a Hindu reform movement his father helped lead, which worshipped one God without images.
That's the nirguna side: God beyond form and qualities. Anything you picture is smaller than God, and the picture can end up being what you worship.

teach.h: SAGUNA: GOD WITH A FACE TO LOVE.
teach.b: Mira sang the saguna side: God with form and qualities, Krishna with his flute, someone you can love, dance for, even argue with. Love needs a face, that side says; people love what they can speak to.
Gitanjali sits between them, speaking to God as you, close as breath, with no image at all.
Readers still argue which side he's on. Either way, the book's own name tells you what the songs are for. Where others bring flowers to the altar, a poet holds out songs.

how: Tagore's songs, known in Bengali as Rabindrasangeet, are still sung in Bengal at home, in school and at gatherings; readers in English meet them through Gitanjali, his own prose versions.

games.q: your friend says singing to God as 'you' is pretend, since God has no form. you lean his way. now state the other side's best case.
o: love needs someone to speak to; the saguna side says God takes a form we can love.
there isn't one: Tagore's Brahmo upbringing settled the question against images.
Tagore won the Nobel singing 'thou,' so that way of singing must be right.
games.why: the saguna view, Mira's side: people love what they can address, so God can have a face. the nirguna side answers that any face is smaller than God.

practice: Say his line slowly, out loud: when thou commandest me to sing it seems that my heart would break with pride. Then sit with it for two minutes.
Let the thou be a face, a presence, or simply a question; each one has a side in this debate, and each has been sung for a long time.

wordCard.voice: The Nobel poet: Rabindranath Tagore, the Bengali poet and songwriter who put his own devotional songs into English and called the book Song Offerings.

orig.note: Bengali: Gitanjali, the book's name. Tagore's English title page gives it as Song Offerings.

carryVoice: Your line: song offerings. Instead of flowers on the altar, a poet holds out his songs. Until tomorrow.
